title: Tokenization & Subword Units
oneLineScope: The vocabulary problem and its subword answer: BPE, WordPiece, and SentencePiece, with a concrete walk-through of the merge algorithm.
prose:
Where we are. The encoder–decoder contrast node traced how architectural choices — bidirectional versus autoregressive reading, full attention versus causal masking — shape what a model can do. Those choices live entirely in the world of tensors, embeddings, and weight matrices. But before a single matrix multiply can happen, the raw string that arrives as input must be converted into a sequence of discrete symbols. This node covers that conversion: the step the architecture completely depends on yet rarely discusses.

The gist. Tokenization is the process of turning a string of characters into a sequence of integers — indices into a fixed vocabulary. The challenge is choosing a vocabulary that is compact enough to be learned well, yet broad enough to represent any text the model will ever see. The field settled on subword tokenization: frequent words are kept whole; rare or novel words are split into reusable fragments, providing near-universal coverage without an impractically large vocabulary. Three families — BPE, WordPiece, and SentencePiece — share that philosophy but differ in how they build the vocabulary and in whether they require pre-segmented word boundaries at all.

Why it matters. The tokenizer is the silent contract between text and model. It determines sequence length, which controls memory cost (the \(n \times n\) attention score matrix) and what fits in context. It shapes which morphological relationships the model can share across representations. And it is frozen before training begins: a tokenizer cannot be revised once a model has trained on it, making the vocabulary decision one of the few truly irreversible choices in the whole pipeline. Grasping this layer is the prerequisite for understanding what pretraining objectives are actually optimizing — and what the model is blind to.

The vocabulary problem

The most natural choice is word-level tokenization: one vocabulary entry per word type. This has the appeal of aligning with linguistic intuition — morphemes, collocations, and distributional properties all operate roughly at the word level. But two problems compound at scale. A vocabulary of \(V\) word types must be enormous to cover English — hundreds of thousands of forms once morphological variants, proper nouns, and technical terms are counted — and the embedding matrix \(E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d_{\text{model}}}\) grows with it. Worse, no finite corpus contains every word form the model will encounter at inference. Out-of-vocabulary (OOV) words receive no embedding; the model is simply blind to them. For morphologically rich languages — Finnish, Turkish, Arabic — OOV is catastrophic: every novel stem–suffix combination is unknown even when stem and suffix are individually frequent.

The opposite extreme is character-level tokenization: one entry per character, OOV eliminated by construction. The vocabulary shrinks to a few hundred entries, but a character-level sequence is roughly five to ten times longer than a word-level one for English, and that cost is quadratic: the \(n \times n\) attention score matrix grows with the square of sequence length. There is also a subtler cost. The relationships between walk, walked, walking, and walker — what a linguist would call inflectional and derivational morphology — become implicit patterns distributed across dozens of character positions rather than compact lexical entries the attention mechanism can address directly.

Subword tokenization occupies the middle ground. Frequent words are kept whole; rare or novel words are split into reusable pieces. The vocabulary is modest — typically 30,000 to 50,000 entries — yet OOV is essentially eliminated, because any unseen word can be decomposed into known subwords, down to individual characters as a last resort.

Here is the connection to morphology worth holding carefully. The pieces that emerge from statistical training often look like morphological units: prefixes, suffixes, stems. A linguist inspecting a BPE vocabulary will find entries like un-, -ness, -ing, and -tion that correspond to productive morphs. But the algorithm has no access to a morphological grammar; it is optimizing raw frequency, not linguistic structure. Frequent morphological affixes are, almost by definition, frequent substrings, so BPE and its relatives rediscover them from the data. The correspondence is real but approximate — the algorithm will also merge across morphological boundaries when frequency warrants it, and will leave morphologically motivated splits unmade when they are not frequent enough. The vocabulary of a trained tokenizer reads like a rough morpheme inventory, but it was assembled by a greedy statistics procedure, not by a linguist. This is useful for building intuition, and potentially a useful inductive bias for transfer, but it would be wrong to describe the tokenizer as performing morphological analysis.

Byte-Pair Encoding

BPE (Sennrich, Haddow, and Birch, 2016) adapted a 1994 lossless-compression algorithm to the vocabulary-construction problem. The procedure is simple enough to trace by hand.

Initialization. Represent each word in the training corpus as a sequence of characters, appending a special end-of-word marker (so low becomes l o w </w>). Count word frequencies.

Merge loop. At each step, scan all adjacent symbol pairs across all word representations and count co-occurrences weighted by word frequency. Find the most frequent pair; merge it everywhere into a single new symbol; add that symbol to the vocabulary. Repeat until the vocabulary reaches target size \(V\).

A small example makes the mechanics concrete. Suppose the training corpus contains low (frequency 5), lower (2), newest (6), widest (3). After character initialization, the symbol inventory is {l, o, w, e, r, n, s, t, i, d, </w>}. The most frequent adjacent pair is e s (in newest and widest, weighted count 9); merge to es. Then es </w>; merge to es</w>. Then l o (count 7) merges to lo; then lo w merges to low. After a handful of steps the representations read low</w>, low er</w>, n ew es</w>, w id es</w> — frequent stems and suffixes have emerged as units. Run this to 30,000–50,000 merges on a large corpus and you have a practical subword vocabulary.

What BPE optimizes is raw pair frequency, not any linguistic criterion. The merges are greedy and irreversible; the vocabulary reflects the distributional properties of the training corpus, not a grammar.

WordPiece

WordPiece (Schuster and Nakajima, 2012; used by BERT) uses the same merge-loop skeleton but replaces the frequency criterion with a likelihood criterion. At each step it merges the pair \((A, B)\) that maximizes \(P(AB) / (P(A) \cdot P(B))\) — the pair whose joint occurrence is most surprising relative to independent unigram frequencies. This is a pointwise mutual information criterion. It tends to prefer merges that produce units with non-compositional distributions, which often (though not always) align better with meaningful morphological units. In practice, BPE and WordPiece produce similar vocabularies for high-resource languages; differences surface most in morphologically complex or low-resource settings where the frequency and surprise criteria diverge.

SentencePiece

Both BPE and WordPiece require that text has already been pre-tokenized into words — split on spaces. That assumption breaks for Japanese, Chinese, Korean, and Thai, and it encodes language-specific preprocessing decisions that can differ across pipelines. SentencePiece (Kudo and Richardson, 2018) removes the pre-tokenization step by operating on the raw text stream including whitespace. It treats a space as just another character (marking it with ◁ to keep tokenization invertible) and can apply either a BPE or a Unigram LM algorithm over this raw stream.

The Unigram LM variant (Kudo, 2018) takes a fundamentally different angle: start with a large candidate vocabulary, then prune it by removing symbols whose removal least reduces training-corpus log-likelihood under a unigram model. The model assigns each possible segmentation of a word a probability proportional to the product of token unigram probabilities, sums over all segmentations via a forward algorithm, and updates token probabilities by EM. The structure is closely related to the probabilistic segmentation models familiar from morphological analysis, and it yields a probability distribution over segmentations rather than a single deterministic split — a property that can be exploited for data augmentation during training.

Trade-offs and practical notes

Vocabulary size \(V\) is the central design dial. A larger \(V\) keeps more words whole — shorter sequences, lower attention cost — but demands a larger embedding matrix \(E \in \mathbb{R}^{V \times d_{\text{model}}}\) and requires more training data per entry to learn reliable representations. In the era covered here: GPT-2 used byte-level BPE with \(V = 50{,}257\); BERT used WordPiece with \(V = 30{,}522\); T5 used SentencePiece with \(V = 32{,}000\).

One consequence worth noting: tokens are not words. A 500-word passage might tokenize to 650 or 750 tokens depending on vocabulary and language. The model’s context window — its \(n\), the number of positions it can attend over — is a token count, not a word count. Morphologically rich text consumes context faster than English text in the same window.

Byte-level BPE, used by GPT-2, takes the fallback idea to its logical limit: the base vocabulary is the 256 byte values, guaranteeing that any UTF-8 input is representable without an unknown-token symbol. Rare scripts and emoji decompose into byte tokens; common English words merge all the way to word-level entries. This completeness property is why GPT-2’s tokenizer was carried forward essentially unchanged into GPT-3.

Where it leads

Pretraining objectives takes the tokenized sequence — now a sequence of integer IDs — as given, and asks what loss function should drive training. The tokenizer is the boundary between raw text and the discrete sequence the model sees; understanding it clarifies exactly what the model is predicting when it assigns a probability to the next token, and what structural information it has and has not been given. The vocabulary size \(V\) also directly sets the output dimension of the final projection layer and the width of the embedding table, so the tokenizer’s choices thread through the whole model specification.

diagrams.caption: The BPE merge process on a toy set of words: successive most-frequent pair merges reduce character sequences to subword tokens, and each merge adds one entry to the vocabulary.
diagrams.altText: Four stages left to right. Stage 0: individual characters l, o, w, e, s, t plus end-of-word marker. Stage 1: merge 'es' (most frequent pair) to form a single token. Stage 2: merge 'lo' to form a single token. Stage 3: merge 'low' (lo+w) to form the final subword tokens. Each merge step is annotated with the pair merged and the growing vocabulary list.
diagrams.prompt: Structural diagram showing the BPE merge process on a toy corpus containing the words 'low' (freq 5), 'lower' (freq 2), 'newest' (freq 6), 'widest' (freq 3). Show four stages arranged left to right. Stage 0 (leftmost): the word 'lowest' written as individual character tokens: l · o · w · e · s · t · </w>, each in its own small box. Above, label 'Stage 0: characters'. Stage 1: highlight the pair 'e s' as most frequent (freq 9); merge it into a single box 'es'. Annotate: 'merge: e + s → es'. Stage 2: highlight 'lo' as next most frequent; merge into 'lo'. Annotate: 'merge: l + o → lo'. Stage 3: merge 'lo' + 'w' into 'low'. Annotate: 'merge: lo + w → low'. Final result: boxes reading 'low', 'es</w>' (or similar). On the right, show a small growing vocabulary list with entries added at each merge step. Emphasize: each merge adds exactly one vocabulary entry. Keep token boxes in blue (the thing under construction); the merged pair at each step in red (the key step); the vocabulary list in green (the output).

diagrams.caption: Subword tokenization in practice: a common word stays whole with one vocabulary ID; a rare or novel word splits into reusable subword pieces, each with its own ID and embedding row.
diagrams.altText: Two examples side by side. Left: the common word 'low' is assigned a single vocabulary ID (e.g. 3482), kept whole. Right: the rare word 'unhappiness' is split into three subword pieces: 'un' (ID 291), 'happi' (ID 7104), 'ness' (ID 512), each carrying its own embedding row. A note below explains that subwords like 'un-' and '-ness' approximate morphemes but were learned from frequency, not grammar.
diagrams.prompt: Structural diagram showing two side-by-side tokenization examples. Left example: the common word 'low' is kept as a single token, assigned one vocabulary ID (e.g. 3482). Show the word in a single box with its ID below it. Right example: the rare or novel word 'unhappiness' is split into three subword pieces: 'un' (vocabulary ID 291), 'happi' (vocabulary ID 7104), 'ness' (vocabulary ID 512). Show each piece in its own box with its ID below it. Add a note below the right example reading: 'un- and -ness approximate morphemes — but these units were learned from frequency, not grammar'. Emphasize the single-token common word in blue (compact, whole); the subword pieces of the rare word in red (split, decomposed); vocabulary IDs in muted grey below each box.

bibliography.citation: Sennrich, R., Haddow, B., & Birch, A. (2016). "Neural Machine Translation of Rare Words with Subword Units." ACL. arXiv:1508.07909.
bibliography.annotation: The paper that introduced BPE for NMT vocabulary construction. §3 describes the merge algorithm; §4 contains the toy example this node adapts. Essential primary source for BPE.

bibliography.citation: Kudo, T., & Richardson, J. (2018). "SentencePiece: A simple and language independent subword tokenizer and detokenizer for Neural Text Processing." EMNLP. arXiv:1808.06226.
bibliography.annotation: Introduces the SentencePiece framework: raw-text processing, ▁ whitespace marker, and language-agnostic operation. §2 covers the framework; the companion paper (Kudo 2018, arXiv:1804.10959) covers the Unigram LM algorithm, including the EM-based pruning procedure.

bibliography.citation: Hugging Face NLP Course. "Summary of the tokenizers." (online, accessed 2024).
bibliography.annotation: Clear side-by-side comparison of BPE, WordPiece, and Unigram LM training algorithms with worked examples. Best quick reference for the differences between the three families. Practical depth, no derivations.

bibliography.citation: Jurafsky, D., & Martin, J. H. Speech and Language Processing (3rd ed., draft). Chapter 2.
bibliography.annotation: Chapter 2 of SLP3 covers tokenization and normalization with the linguistically careful framing most appropriate for this reader. Good on the word-boundary problem for non-space-delimited languages and on the relationship between tokenization decisions and downstream model behavior.
